references.text: Pharaoh expresses his ignorance of the Lord and refuses to obey his command to let Israel go.
God says that the Egyptians will know that he is the Lord, in response to Pharaoh's question about who the Lord is.
Through the plagues, Pharaoh will come to know that God is the Lord, as a direct answer to his ignorance.
The Lord sets apart Goshen so that Pharaoh may know that he is the Lord in the midst of the land.
God explains that he has raised up Pharaoh to show his power and proclaim his name throughout all the earth.
God will glorify himself through Pharaoh so that the Egyptians will know that he is the Lord.
The Egyptians will know that God is the Lord when he glorifies himself through Pharaoh and his army.
Job refers to God as the one who does great things beyond understanding, similar to how God revealed himself to Pharaoh.
God speaks of knowing him and his sovereignty over nations, in contrast to Pharaoh's ignorance.
A prophecy against Pharaoh that compares his pride with that of the Pharaoh who did not know the Lord.
Paul cites the event with Pharaoh to demonstrate God's sovereignty and how God used Pharaoh's hardness.
Connects Pharaoh's denial in 5:2 directly to God's plan of judgment as a response in 7:4.
Shows the development of Pharaoh's resistance from total denial (5:2) to attempts at compromise (10:8).
Contrasts Pharaoh's total refusal in 5:2 with his willingness to compromise in 8:24, demonstrating hardening.
Moses' doubt in 6:12 is a direct response to Pharaoh's denial in 5:2.
The servants' question in 10:7 highlights the consequence of Pharaoh's 'I do not know' from 5:2.
10:3 (or the message there) represents God's demand that Pharaoh directly refuses to acknowledge in 5:2.
